page: Amazon Web Services m1.large is a legacy first-generation general-purpose instance deployed on the Xen hypervisor. It features two dedicated physical cores powered by an Intel Xeon E5-2651 v2 processor running at 1.8 GHz on an x86_64 architecture. The system provides 8.0 GB of system memory, yielding 3.75 GB per core, and includes 840 GB of local HDD storage along with a baseline network bandwidth of 1 Gbps. It contains no specialized hardware accelerators, such as GPUs. Instruction set support is restricted, featuring AES cryptographic extensions but lacking modern vector and matrix acceleration instructions like AVX, AVX-512, and AMX.

Benchmark measurements position the m1.large firmly in the lowest tier of overall system performance across all standard evaluations. In computational tasks, it delivers a single-core Geekbench score of 475.0 and a multi-core score of 630.0, alongside a PassMark CPU score of 1378.1 and a stress-ng multi-core value of 1591.77. Memory throughput reaches 11.1 GB/sec for uncached large block reads and 9.52 GB/sec for writes. Database operations under PassMark register at 662.02, while Redis SET operations achieve 0.62 million operations per second, placing memory, computational, and storage operations within the bottom 10% benchmark segment.

Given its older hardware generation, low core frequency, and spindle-based magnetic local disks, the m1.large offers poor qualitative resource and compute efficiency relative to modern general-purpose alternatives. Workloads requiring vector extensions, high IOPS, or parallel computing throughput will experience heavy bottlenecks. This instance is primarily limited to legacy maintenance, low-traffic static web servers, simple staging environments, or internal non-critical tasks that require substantial local HDD capacity without heavy compute demands.
description: Amazon Web Services m1.large is a first-generation general-purpose server powered by an Intel Xeon E5-2651 v2 processor with two dedicated cores at 1.8 GHz on the Xen hypervisor. Equipped with 8.0 GB of RAM, 840 GB of local HDD storage, and a 1 Gbps network baseline, the instance operates without a GPU and lacks AVX instruction set extensions. Benchmark testing indicates legacy-tier performance across compute and memory vectors, placing stress-ng, Geekbench (630.0 multi-core), and PassMark CPU (1378.1) scores in the bottom decile. With 0.62 million Redis SET operations per second and uncached memory read bandwidth of 11.1 GB/sec, its older architecture presents limited computational efficiency compared to contemporary platforms. Consequently, m1.large is best suited for low-load static web serving, non-critical background utilities, and legacy application hosting.
